analysis.one_liner: Requires employers with 15 or more workers to provide up to seven paid sick days a year.
analysis.headline: Despite 106 cosponsors, the bill never received a vote in any House committee or on the House floor in the 110th Congress.
analysis.plain_summary: The Healthy Families Act would have required employers with 15 or more employees to provide paid sick leave: seven days a year for full-time workers, and a prorated amount for people working 20 or more hours a week. Workers could use the time for their own illness or medical care, or to care for a sick child, spouse, or parent. The bill was introduced in March 2007 and referred to three House committees, then to two subcommittees, but no committee ever voted on it and it never came to the House floor.
analysis.who_benefits: Workers who had no paid sick leave — disproportionately low-wage workers, part-timers, and caregivers. The bill's findings noted that 79 percent of families in the lowest earnings quartile lacked paid sick leave, and that workers who must go to a job sick or send a sick child to school lose pay or lose health. Workers at covered businesses who already earned paid leave would keep their existing, more generous policies, because the bill barred employers from cutting existing leave to comply.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Low-wage workers without paid sick leave

how_it_helps.text: Employers with 15 or more employees must provide at least seven paid sick days a year to workers averaging 30 or more hours a week, and prorated leave for those working 20 to 30 hours.
Leave can be used for the worker's own illness, injury, preventive or diagnostic care, or to care for a child, spouse, parent, or close family equivalent.
Employers may not eliminate, reduce, or redesignate leave already in existence to comply, and more generous existing policies are preserved; the bill sets a floor, not a ceiling.

The bill prohibits employers from firing, demoting, or retaliating against workers for using sick leave, and lets workers sue or file complaints with the Labor Department, with reinstatement and back pay available as remedies.

The bill's findings cite public-health benefits: workers who can stay home when sick or care for a sick child reduce the spread of contagious illness in schools and child care, and early routine care lowers later emergency-care costs.

analysis.who_pays: Covered employers — businesses and public agencies with 15 or more employees — bear the cost of up to seven days of paid leave per full-time worker per year, plus recordkeeping and enforcement requirements. That cost falls most directly on sectors with many hourly workers and little existing paid leave, such as retail, food service, and hospitality, which would pay wages for time not worked or raise prices to cover it. Employers with fewer than 15 employees are exempt.

drawbacks.text: Covered employers absorb the wage cost of up to seven paid days per full-time worker each year, the steepest adjustment for retail, restaurant, and hospitality businesses that historically offered little or no paid leave; the bill's own findings argue the cost is offset by lower turnover, less lost productivity from workers coming in sick, and reduced emergency-care spending.

Employers may require a health care provider's certification for any leave spanning more than three consecutive workdays, which puts a burden on workers to obtain documentation; the bill directs regulators to set a process for workers who have no health insurance, but the requirement could still deter some short absences.
Businesses with fewer than 15 employees — where paid sick leave is least common — are entirely exempt, so many of the workers who most lacked paid leave would have gotten no benefit from this bill.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: For the roughly half of American workers who lacked paid sick leave at the time — and the roughly 80 percent of the lowest-earning quartile — the benefit is direct: income protection when sick and the ability to care for a child without losing a job or pay. The cost is real but limited: a wage floor of seven days is about 2.7 percent of an annual work schedule, applies only to employers of 15 or more, and protects existing benefits rather than allowing cuts. The main design weakness is the 15-employee threshold, which excludes the smallest employers where paid leave is rarest. Overall, the tradeoff favors workers, with the cost borne by their employers.

outcome.mechanism: The bill sat in three House committees and two subcommittees from June 2007 until the Congress ended in January 2009 — no subcommittee, full committee, or floor vote ever happened.

narrative.text: Rep. Rosa DeLauro (D-CT) introduced the Healthy Families Act on March 15, 2007, with 12 original cosponsors including Rep. George Miller of California, the chair of the House Education and Labor Committee.
The bill was referred to the Committees on Education and Labor, Oversight and Government Reform, and House Administration.

On June 27, 2007, it was referred to the Subcommittee on Workforce Protections and the Subcommittee on Health, Employment, Labor, and Pensions; no further action of any kind appears in the record for the rest of the 110th Congress.
By the end of the Congress the bill had 106 cosponsors, all of them Democrats; no Republican cosponsored it, and it never received a vote in committee or on the House floor.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Employers of 15 or more employees that provided little or no paid sick leave kept that payroll saving for the full two years the bill sat without a vote, while the workers without paid leave remained without it.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Employers without paid sick leave obligations

for.name: Rosa DeLauro
for.what_they_did: Introduced the Healthy Families Act and built Democratic cosponsorship.

for.name: 106 House Democrats
for.what_they_did: Cosponsored the bill — every cosponsor was a Democrat.

for.name: George Miller
for.role: Chair, House Education and Labor Committee
for.what_they_did: Was an original cosponsor; his committee received the primary referral but never reported the bill out.

against.name: House Education and Labor Committee
against.role: Primary committee of referral; House had a Democratic majority
against.what_they_did: Took no recorded action on the bill after its June 2007 referral to two subcommittees; no markup, no vote, no report to the floor in the remaining 18 months of the Congress.

against.name: House leadership
against.what_they_did: Never brought the bill to the House floor or scheduled it; the bill's action history ends with subcommittee referrals.

against.name: U.S. Chamber of Commerce and business coalitions
against.what_they_did: Opposed paid sick leave mandates as a burden on employers, arguing they raise labor costs; no member of either party moved the bill forward during the Congress.

sides.party_line_note: All 106 cosponsors were Democrats and none of the 202 House Republicans signed on; the bill died without any vote, so no roll call shows the split.

industries.industry: Retail, food service, and hospitality employers
industries.note: These sectors employ many hourly workers with little or no paid sick leave, so the mandate's wage cost would fall hardest on them — and the benefit would go to their own workers, who currently lose pay or jobs when they get sick.

industries.industry: Covered employers (15 or more employees) generally
industries.note: All covered employers would pay up to seven days of leave per full-time worker, but the bill's findings cite offsetting gains from lower turnover, less presenteeism, and fewer emergency-care costs; employers already offering equivalent leave would have had to change nothing.
Exempt from the mandate entirely, they would face no new obligation while their larger competitors absorbed the leave cost — but their own workers would get no new paid leave either.
